title: Bring Your Own Device
summary: Bring your own device is the policy and technical model in which staff use personally owned phones, tablets, or laptops for work, with the organisation granting access to corporate data on hardware it does not own or fully control. The model inverts the usual assumption behind endpoint security, because the device may be unmanaged, shared with family members, running an outdated operating system, or already compromised, so protections must be enforced through the applications and data rather than through a machine the company images and patches itself. The usual control set separates work from personal use with a managed profile or container, enforces device encryption, screen lock, and a minimum platform version before mail or documents are reachable, and registers the device in a management service so access can be revoked and corporate data wiped without erasing personal content. The arrangement also needs a written policy covering which device types are supported, what the organisation may inspect or remove, who pays for connectivity, and what happens when someone leaves. The common mistake is to approve personal devices without enrolment and conditional access, which leaves corporate mail on an unmanaged phone that no one can revoke, audit, or wipe after theft.

beginner.definition: Bring your own device means people use their own phone or laptop for work. The company gives access to work email and files on that personal device. The company does not own the device, so it must protect its data in other ways. Rules are needed to keep work and private life separate.
beginner.whyItMatters: Personal devices may miss security updates or be shared with family members. If the device is lost, work email and files can be exposed. An infected personal phone can carry that problem into the company network. Staff also worry about their employer touching private photos and messages. Clear rules solve both problems and keep people productive.
howItWorks: The company decides which device types are allowed and what protection each must have.
You enrol the device in a management service that can apply company rules.
Work data sits in a separate container so private apps cannot reach it.
The company requires a screen lock, encryption, and a recent operating system.
Access to email and files is granted only after the device meets those rules.
If the device is lost or the person leaves, the company removes only its own data.
beginner.example: Think of a post office counter that allows staff to bring their own cash box. The counter provides a locked drawer fixed to the desk for office money. Private belongings stay in the staff bag, untouched. If a worker leaves, the office opens its own drawer and takes back only what belongs to it. The separation keeps both sides safe.
takeaways: Separate work data into a container so personal content stays private.
Use device enrolment and access rules so a lost phone can be handled quickly.
Write down what the company may inspect or wipe before anyone signs up.

objectives: Explain what bring your own device means and how it differs from company-issued hardware.
Describe the main risks that personal devices introduce to corporate data.
Explain how containers and mobile device management separate work from personal data.
Describe how enrolment and conditional access gate access to company resources.
Explain the privacy commitments, such as selective wipe, that a policy should state.
Outline what happens to company data when a device is lost or an employee leaves.
